A.title: Mozambique Online Casino Rules Take Effect 20 November
A.excerpt: Decree 61/2026 opens online casino concessions to Mozambican public companies with 26% local ownership and a .mz-only model.
body: Mozambique's Regulation on the Operation and Practice of Online Games of Chance, approved by Decree No. 61/2026 of 21 September, enters into force on 20 November 2026, sixty days after publication. As reported by iGaming Business, entry into force is not a commercial launch: no date has been set for applications to open, and the regulator, the General Inspectorate of Games (IGJ), has yet to publish several implementing details. The decree nonetheless gives the clearest picture so far of how Mozambique intends to structure a domestic online market, and it is considerably more protective of local participation than most African frameworks.

Eligibility is narrow. Only public limited companies incorporated under Mozambican law may hold a concession, and more than one concessionaire is permitted. Two categories qualify: operators of physical casinos in Mozambique, and licensed betting and online gaming operators that meet the new requirements. A physical casino is not a precondition. Where shareholders are companies, at least 26 per cent of paid-up share capital must be held by Mozambican-registered shareholders, and that stake cannot be reduced without prior authorisation. Foreign operators should therefore expect to enter through a local joint venture, and the shareholder agreement will need to deal carefully with the locked-in 26 per cent.

The financial thresholds are significant. Minimum share capital is MZN 100 million, or a higher figure set by the regulator. Initial guarantees total MZN 25 million: MZN 15 million to secure legal obligations including player balances and potential fines, and MZN 10 million to secure the special online gambling tax. Guarantees may take the form of bank deposits or autonomous bank guarantees and are reviewed after six months. Licences run for up to three years for physical casino concessionaires and two years for other applicants, which makes renewal risk a real commercial consideration when valuing an entry.

Revenue-sharing is handled through two separate contractual contributions, each at a minimum of 2.5 per cent of annual gross revenue after winnings, one for social and public-responsibility purposes and one for tourism development outside gambling. The regulation treats these as contractual obligations rather than taxes, and concession contracts may set higher rates. The decree does not state a gambling tax rate and instead refers to existing fiscal legislation, while licence and concession-award fees are to be set elsewhere. Business plans cannot be finalised until those figures are known, and applicants should seek early clarity from the authorities.

The technical and payments model is strongly localised. Authorised sites must use the .mz domain, and access from Mozambique or by Mozambique-registered accounts must be redirected to the national site. Accounts may be funded only through payment instruments authorised by the Bank of Mozambique and denominated in meticais; foreign-issued instruments and currency conversion are excluded. Withdrawals must be paid within 48 hours, operators must hold enough funds to cover all player balances, gambling data must be stored in Mozambique for at least ten years, and systems must be certified and audited annually. Operators used to a single global platform will need a ring-fenced local stack.

Player protection rules are detailed. Players must set daily, weekly and monthly deposit limits at registration; reductions apply immediately and increases only after 24 hours. Under-18s are barred, age verification must be automatic, and self-exclusion lasts at least three months. Permitted games include baccarat, blackjack, roulette, poker, slots, keno, instant games and bingo, with other types needing ministerial approval. Applications must be filed in Portuguese with the tourism authority, so translation and local filing capacity should be arranged at the outset.

Enforcement reaches beyond licensees. The regulation applies to gambling aimed at Mozambique regardless of the operator's nationality or server location, and the IGJ may order unlicensed operators to stop and remove services within 48 hours, after which network intermediaries are notified and generally have 48 hours to block access. Affiliates, payment providers and hosting companies should therefore review their Mozambique exposure before 20 November. Because the details come from trade reporting, the decree text and any IGJ circulars should be reviewed before advice is given.

A.title: GRAI Targets Dozens of Unlicensed Operators in Ireland
A.excerpt: Ireland's regulator says dozens of black-market operators have been warned since July, while an ESRI survey shows cross-product play.
body: The Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI) has told the Irish Times that since July it has acted against dozens of unlicensed operators, ranging from small Irish bookmakers to major online brands and the two largest prediction markets in the world. In an interview published on 4 November 2026, chief executive Anne Marie Caulfield said that most of these businesses stopped after receiving initial cease-and-desist warnings. The authority has not yet gone to the High Court. The comments offer an early view of how the new regulator, which began licensing online bookmakers in 2026 under the Gambling Regulation Act 2024, intends to use its powers.

The enforcement model is deliberately graduated. GRAI can issue cease-and-desist letters and, if those fail, seek High Court orders. The practical effect is that the regulator achieves most of its aims through correspondence, which keeps costs low but places weight on the credibility of the court route. Unlicensed operators receiving a letter should assume that continued service to Irish customers risks proceedings, and counsel should advise on the commercial cost of withdrawing against the cost of litigating in Ireland. The reference to prediction markets suggests that GRAI regards event-contract platforms as within its remit when they are offered to Irish residents.

The regulator also emphasised that unlicensed businesses often skip safeguards that apply to licensed firms, including the ban on credit card use and age checks. That framing is consistent with the arguments being made by regulators across Europe: that the black market is a consumer-protection problem and not only a revenue problem. For licensed operators it reinforces the competitive case for enforcement, and for payment providers it signals that Irish customers' transactions with unlicensed brands may attract attention.

A survey by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI), commissioned by GRAI and published on 4 November, adds evidence for the policy debate. Based on 1,000 respondents, it found that almost four in ten people who open online accounts for horse racing or sport later gamble on other forms such as casino games, slots and lotteries. About 10 per cent had four or more accounts, one in seven said emails or app notifications prompted their latest session, and 26 per cent of online gamblers reported losing a lot of money in their latest session against 17 per cent of in-person gamblers. These figures are survey-based and should be quoted with that caveat.

The researchers identified a clear asymmetry between how easily people deposit and open accounts and how hard it is to withdraw and close them. That finding links directly to consumer complaints now reaching GRAI, many of which concern difficulty getting money back from online bookmakers. The Act requires licensees to respond promptly to payment requests and to close accounts when asked. Operators should audit withdrawal and account-closure journeys, complaint handling times and cross-sell triggers, since these are the areas where a regulator already holding complaint data is most likely to look first.

Looking forward, GRAI plans a social impact fund, to which licensed operators will contribute, from next year, and is working with the largest operators on a national self-exclusion system. The Irish Bookmakers Association has welcomed the report. For operators, the combination of marketing-prompt data, multi-account findings and a planned self-exclusion scheme suggests that direct marketing and cross-product promotion will be a focus of future guidance or conditions.

The practical agenda for counsel is therefore threefold: confirm licensing status and the position of any Irish-facing brands, review marketing triggers and cross-selling against the survey findings, and prepare for the self-exclusion and social-fund obligations. Because the interview does not give a numerical count of the operators contacted or any statutory citations for the actions taken, advisers should request the underlying notices when acting for a recipient.

A.title: UKGC Illegal Gambling Index Shows Low but Harmful Use
A.excerpt: The UKGC's new index finds 2.5% of past-year gamblers used illegal sites in four weeks, with a harm-prone subgroup.
body: The Gambling Commission has published the first results of its Illegal Gambling Index, developed with Yonder Consulting and reported by NEXT.io on 5 November 2026. The index combines seven self-reported behavioural indicators, such as using sites not registered with GamStop, registering with sites that skip age or identity checks, and using a VPN or cryptocurrency to access gambling. The behaviours are weighted by recency, separating the previous four weeks, the previous 12 months and older activity. The initial findings use year one of the Gambling Survey for Great Britain, covering April 2025 to April 2026.

The headline numbers are modest. Among people who gambled in the past year, 2.5 per cent used illegal sites in the previous four weeks and a further 1.5 per cent did so in the 12 months but not the last four weeks. Among all respondents, including non-gamblers, the figures are 0.6 per cent and 0.4 per cent. A further 4.6 per cent of all respondents showed limited indications of engagement but could not be confidently classified as users. The Commission's executive director for operations, Sue Young, described the results as mixed: engagement appears low and stable overall, but a subgroup of online gamblers using these sites is more likely to experience harm.

The demographic detail matters for policy. Use was higher among men than women and, over the past 12 months, most common among adults aged 18 to 24, while among those aged 25 to 34 it was more concentrated in the previous four weeks. Among 12-month users, the most frequent indicators were using a site not registered with GamStop (58 per cent) and cancelling a withdrawal before the funds arrived (56.6 per cent). The second figure is a reminder that product design on licensed sites, including reverse-withdrawal features, can interact with the pull of unlicensed alternatives.

The index should be read alongside the Commission's earlier open banking research, which suggested that illegal gambling supplements rather than replaces licensed play. Together the two studies challenge the narrative that regulatory tightening drives large numbers of customers offshore. They do not, however, remove the industry's concern about the harm profile of the small group who do use illegal sites, and the Commission is clearly building an evidence base to support continued enforcement and to resist arguments for loosening requirements.

The caveats are important and the Commission itself has stressed them. The findings are initial and rest on one year of survey data, the indicators are self-reported, those with limited indications were excluded from user figures, and the effect of recent disruption activity cannot yet be measured. The Commission reported a substantial increase in disruption activity in the second quarter of 2026/27 but said it is too early to assess its impact. Practitioners citing the numbers in submissions should therefore present them as indicative.

The next steps announced are of direct relevance to compliance teams. The Commission plans to expand its Illegal Gambling Data Dashboard to cover affiliates, social media, advertisers, payment providers and hosting services, and to develop further engagement measures that separate short-term fluctuations from long-term trends. An expanded dashboard implies more systematic identification of enablers, and affiliates and payment providers should expect greater scrutiny of any links to unlicensed brands.

For licensed operators, the immediate lessons are practical. Review the withdrawal-reversal function in light of the survey evidence, ensure that GamStop integration and customer interaction processes are working consistently, and document how information about customers' wider gambling activity is used within data protection limits. Operators that can demonstrate a considered, evidence-led approach to the illegal market are better placed in any later supervisory discussion.

A.title: Brazil SPA Agenda: Sanctions and Bettor Compensation in Q4
A.excerpt: Brazil's 2026/27 betting agenda puts a sanctions review and bettor compensation procedures in Q4, with AML review in early 2027.
body: Brazil's Secretariat of Prizes and Bets (SPA) published its 2026/27 regulatory agenda on 12 February 2026, formalised by Normative Ordinance No. 408 in the Official Gazette the following day. With the final quarter of 2026 now under way, the agenda's last items for the year deserve attention from operators and their advisers. These are better monitoring and inspection procedures, a review of the sanctions regime, and procedures for compensating bettors harmed by operators that break the rules. All three suggest that the regulator is moving from licensing the market to policing its conduct.

The sanctions review is the most consequential. Operators have so far operated under a framework in which penalties are set by existing ordinances, and a review may recalibrate how violations are classified and graded. Licence holders should assess their compliance records, document remedial action, and review contractual exposure to sanctions, including in agreements with affiliates and payment partners. Any consultation on the topic should be watched closely, since the timing and form of the review are not specified in the agenda.

Bettor compensation is a newer concept. The agenda refers to procedures for compensating bettors harmed by operators that breach the rules, which implies a mechanism beyond administrative fines. How such compensation would be funded, who decides it, and how it would interact with consumer-protection claims in the courts are open questions. Operators should map customer-complaint handling, unclaimed balances and dispute processes now, so that they can respond quickly when a draft emerges.

The earlier quarters of the agenda set the direction. The first quarter covered the review of licensing criteria (approvals, rejections, suspensions and terminations), payment-blocking procedures for suspected illegal betting including Ordinance No. 566, and affiliate advertising rules. The second quarter addressed regulation of fixed-odds sports betting and other lottery modalities sold through physical terminals, and the third quarter responsible gambling, including a tool allowing bettors to view and monitor their own gambling. This sequence shows a consistent theme of tightening access and traceability.

Looking into 2027, the agenda lists an evaluation of anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing policies in early 2027, an update of procedures for the early collection of popular savings in the second quarter, and a review of the regulations for Caixa Loterias lottery products in the third quarter. The AML review will be of particular interest to operators with cross-border payment flows and to banks and payment institutions serving them, as it may harmonise expectations across licensees.

The political context adds uncertainty. Reporting indicates that Acting SPA chief Daniele Correa Cardoso signed the ordinance after Regis Dudena stepped down, and that a Senate committee has advanced a bill that would ban gambling ads across major media and sports sponsorships. Caixa also delayed the launch of its sports betting brand amid political pressure. Pending legislation could override or accelerate parts of the regulator's agenda, so scenario planning should cover both outcomes.

The agenda is a statement of intent and not a binding timetable, and items may slip. Advisers should check the current SPA site for consultations and ordinances before relying on the quarters described here. In the meantime, operators should prepare for the Q4 topics by auditing complaint data, reviewing compliance with existing monitoring obligations and ensuring that their anti-money-laundering frameworks are ready for scrutiny in 2027.

A.title: Belgium's Blacklist Targets Mirror Sites and Brand Spoofs
A.excerpt: Belgium's Gaming Commission uses dynamic injunctions to block mirror domains and lookalikes of licensed brands.
body: Belgium's Gaming Commission has continued to expand its blacklist of illegal gambling sites, with trade coverage on 5 November 2026 reporting a further batch of 31 sites following a surge in impersonation of the licensed PepperMill Casino brand. We have not reviewed the Commission's own list for that update, so the figures should be verified against the primary source. The episode follows a pattern documented earlier in the year, when the Commission added 22 domains on 21 May 2026, taking the list to more than 890 entries, and illustrates a shift from periodic blacklisting to continuous domain-level enforcement.

The May update shows what the Commission is targeting. According to analysis by Blask, it combined offshore operators without a Belgian licence with domains imitating licensed local brands. After the main BC Game domain was blacklisted in November 2024, the Commission blocked three linked domains. Magnetic Slots lost three, and Stone Vegas and Westace two each. This is the familiar offshore tactic of registering new mirror or country-specific domains to restore access after a block, and the Commission is now treating the practice as a foreseeable event, not a surprise.

The second category is brand spoofing. Blocked lookalikes in May included clones of licensed Belgian brands such as Ladbrokes, bwin and Scooore, and the November reporting links the latest batch to impersonation of PepperMill Casino. Spoofers target popular local brands because players may trust them, which turns the issue into a consumer-fraud problem as much as a licensing one. Licensed operators have a direct commercial interest in monitoring for lookalike domains and in supplying evidence to the Commission.

The legal tool underpinning this approach is the dynamic injunction. According to the Blask analysis, the Commission relies on dynamic injunctions, which extend blocking to new variants of listed sites without a separate legal process for each, and it also cites a new mechanism under Belgium's Code of Economic Law and cooperation with DNS Belgium on fraudulent .be domains. For rights-holders and operators the significance is speed: the interval between a mirror appearing and being blocked can now be short, which narrows the window in which offshore sites profit from the switch.

The scale of activity has increased sharply. Blask reported that since the start of 2026 more than 100 sites had been added to the blacklist, against five in the same period of 2025. Its data for May 2026 put licensed local operators at 94.6 per cent of its index and international operators at 5.39 per cent. Those figures come from a commercial data provider and are not official statistics, but they support the Commission's position that its approach is compatible with a strong licensed market.

Consequences for ordinary players are a continuing legal risk. Belgian law has long provided for penalties for players who use blacklisted sites, and press coverage has referred to fines of up to EUR 25,000, though we have not confirmed the current statutory provisions. Operators and advisers should avoid promoting such sites, and affiliates should remove links to blacklisted domains promptly to reduce the risk of being drawn into enforcement.

For licensed operators, the practical steps are to run brand-protection monitoring, maintain a reporting channel to the Commission and domain registries, and review affiliate contracts for takedown obligations. For offshore businesses, the message is that mirror strategies are unlikely to work for long in Belgium. Payment providers should also screen Belgian-facing merchants against the blacklist, since processing for a listed domain carries both regulatory and reputational risk.
